correctness.rationale: The exact integration-by-parts identity reduces the Fourier-zero equation to Im(e^{ix}Q_p(x))=0. Uniform second-order expansion of Q_p(ps) in inverse p follows from exp(log U/p), with exponential moments of log U controlling the remainder; Gamma(1+is) is uniformly nonzero on compact s ranges. A derivative bound O(1/p) forces the total phase to increase strictly, proving exhaustive simple zeros and the uniform two-term location formula. The digamma series proves strict convexity and exactly one positive phase zero. A centered Weibull third-moment expansion gives the fixed-k zeta(3) term. The proof checks angular Fourier normalization, real p, and endpoints; direct numeric transform tests are supplementary only.

value.rationale: The Fourier zero set of the generalized Gaussian is a natural oscillation invariant, and the singular p->infinity approach to a sharp interval is a motivated noncommuting frequency/shape limit. Instead of a routine fixed-index perturbation, the theorem controls O(p) successive simple zeros uniformly, gives a nontrivial Gamma phase, proves a unique reversal of their sinc-relative displacement, and isolates the zeta(3) skewness effect after mean renormalization. The precise phase and changing sign are not consequences of the classical fixed-p large-frequency results. No stronger global complex-zero theorem is claimed.
